topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Refraction and dispersion between them have carried a printed-diagram question in every P2 paper read for this batch, and the 6-mark banded dispersion question three times (Summer 2021, 2023 and 2026). Summer 2025 Higher Q8 gave 6 marks to a prism drawn point-down; Summer 2024 Foundation Q3 gave 7 across the spectrum, the colour order and the speeds. Prescribed Practical P5 is the physics task Unit 7 Booklet A set in Summer 2021 and 2025, worth 15 marks on its own.
mustMemorise: The normal is at right angles to the surface, and both angles are measured from it
Slower means bent towards the normal; faster means bent away from it
The greater the change of speed, the greater the refraction
The emergent ray from a rectangular block is parallel to the incident ray
The spectrum in order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet
Red is slowed least and refracted least; violet is slowed most and refracted most
Dispersion is the splitting; the band of colours is a spectrum, never a rainbow
P5: the graph of the two angles is a curve, so they are related but not proportional
notOnThisSpec: Total internal reflection, the critical angle and optical fibres
Wave-front diagrams as an assessed skill
The rainbow's full explanation, which needs an internal reflection

note.title: Refraction and dispersion
note.subject: science

mustKnow: Both angles are measured from the normal, the line at right angles to the surface
Slower means bent towards the normal; faster means bent away from it
The greater the change of speed, the greater the refraction
Dispersion splits white light into a spectrum because each colour travels at a different speed in glass; red is slowed and refracted least, violet most
P5: angle of incidence against angle of refraction is a curve, so the two are related but not proportional

notOnThisSpec: Snell's law and refractive index (the specification says a knowledge of Snell's law is not expected)
Total internal reflection, the critical angle and optical fibres
Wave-front diagrams as an assessed skill (AQA Higher only)
The full explanation of a rainbow, which needs an internal reflection as well
Colour by filters, absorption and transmission

mustBeAbleTo: Draw the normal at the point where a ray meets a surface, and measure both angles from it
Turn an angle printed to the surface, outside or inside the material, into an angle from the normal by subtracting from 90 degrees
State which way a ray bends entering and leaving glass or water, and explain it as a change of speed
Say that a ray along the normal has an angle of incidence of 0 degrees and carries straight on
Show why the emergent ray from a rectangular block is parallel to the incident ray
Draw a normal at both faces of a prism, whichever way up it is drawn, and say why its two bends add
Name dispersion and the spectrum, give the seven colours in order from either end, and explain the order by the colours' different speeds in glass
Describe Prescribed Practical P5, plot angle of incidence up against angle of refraction across, and conclude related but not proportional because the graph is a curve
Compare refraction in two materials from their speeds of light: a bigger change of speed gives more refraction
sheet.howExamined: P2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. Refraction arrives as a printed diagram with a mark for each feature: the normal, the direction of the bend, an angle stated, often a ray leaving water or along the normal. Dispersion comes as short answers on a prism diagram and has carried the 6-mark banded question three times (Summer 2021 and 2023 at both tiers, Summer 2026 Foundation). Unit 7 Booklet A has set Prescribed Practical P5 itself (Summer 2021 and 2025): angles measured, a table, a graph with angle of incidence up the side and angle of refraction across, and the conclusion; Booklet B has examined refraction and dispersion in writing (Summer 2023).
traps: Explaining a bend by "optical density" instead of the decrease in speed of the light (Summer 2025 U7 Physics Booklet A H Q1)

Defining refraction without saying that the light passes from one material into another, or not knowing that more refraction means a bigger change of speed (Summer 2023 U7 Physics Booklet B F Q3; H Q1)
Leaving the normal off a prism diagram altogether, or not drawing it at right angles to the face, when the prism is turned point-down (Summer 2025 P2 H Q8)
Bending a ray towards the normal as it leaves the glass, when leaving glass speeds the light up and bends it away (Summer 2025 P2 H Q8)
Putting red at the top of the screen when the prism is drawn point-down: the spectrum flips and violet, refracted most, is at the top (Summer 2025 P2 H Q8)
Writing "refraction" where the answer is dispersion, or "rainbow" where it is spectrum (Summer 2025 P2 F Q2; Summer 2024 P2 F Q3)
Writing "light" where the sentence wants colours: different colours travel at different speeds in glass (Summer 2024 P2 F Q3)
Bending the ray the wrong way as it passes from water into air (Summer 2024 P2 F Q3)

Naming the colours of the spectrum in the wrong order or leaving one out, calling the prism a pyramid or a block, or not saying that the colours travel at different speeds in glass (Summer 2023 P2 F Q7; Summer 2023 P2 H Q2)
Not recalling that violet is refracted most (Summer 2023 U7 Physics Booklet B H Q1)
Showing reflection at the boundary, or drawing the incident and refracted rays on the same side of the normal (Summer 2023 P2 F Q4)
Giving 90 degrees for the angle of incidence of a ray that travels along the normal, where the answer is 0 (Summer 2024 P2 H Q7)
Taking an angle from the surface instead of the normal: the commonest wrong answer in a ray diagram was the complement of the right angle (Summer 2023 P2 F Q1)

Ticking related but not proportional for the P5 graph but giving no reason: most chose the right box, few said that the graph is a curve, not a straight line through the origin (Summer 2025 U7 Physics Booklet A H Q1)
Ruling straight lines from point to point instead of drawing one smooth curve of best fit (Summer 2025 U7 Physics Booklet A Q1)
Leaving the unit off the axis label, when the column heading in the table should match the axis label exactly (Summer 2025 U7 Physics Booklet A Q1)

workedExamples.stem: A diagram shows a ray of light meeting the flat top face of a glass block. The angle between the ray and the surface is marked as 35°. Find the angle of incidence and state which way the ray bends as it enters the glass.

figure.alt: A ray meeting the top face of a glass block with the angle between the ray and the surface marked as 35 degrees, the normal drawn as a dashed line at each face, the ray's path inside the block, and the ray leaving the bottom face.

steps.working: Draw the normal at the point where the ray meets the surface.
steps.decision: Every angle in optics is measured from the normal, so it has to be on the diagram before anything can be read off it.

options: because the normal is the line both angles are measured from
because the normal shows where the block ends
because the normal is the same as the surface
whyMenu.explain: The normal is at right angles to the surface, and the angles of incidence and refraction are both measured from it.

steps.working: The normal and the surface are at right angles, so the printed 35° and the angle of incidence add to 90°.
steps.decision: This is the step that turns a surface angle into an angle of incidence, and it is where most marks are lost.
So the angle of incidence is 55°.

steps.working: The light slows down as it enters the glass.
steps.decision: Slowing down bends a ray towards the normal, so the angle inside the glass is smaller than the angle of incidence.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The angle of incidence is 55°, and the ray bends towards the normal as it enters the glass.

twin.stem: A second diagram marks 40° between the ray and the surface of the same block. State the angle of incidence, in degrees.

figure.alt: A graph of angle of refraction against angle of incidence with six readings plotted, a smooth curve through them and a dashed straight line through the origin.

steps.decision: If the two were proportional, every pair would have the same ratio, so work one out to compare against.

steps.working: Now check the last pair: 70° gives 39°. Doubling the angle of incidence has not doubled the angle of refraction.
steps.decision: The ratio has changed, so the two angles are not in proportion.

steps.working: Plot the points and draw one smooth curve. The curve passes through the origin but bends over as the angle of incidence grows.
steps.decision: The shape is the evidence: a straight line through the origin would have meant proportional.

options: because directly proportional needs a straight line through the origin
because the curve does not reach the top of the grid
because the points are not exactly on the line
whyMenu.explain: Directly proportional means a straight line that passes through the origin. Through the origin on its own is not enough.

steps.working: Write the conclusion in the scheme's words: related but not proportional.
steps.decision: The reason to give is the shape: the graph is a curve, not a straight line through the origin.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: They are related but not proportional: as one increases so does the other, but the graph is a curve rather than a straight line through the origin.

accepted: directly proportional

workedExamples.stem: White light from a ray box passes through a triangular glass prism and lands on a screen. Name the process, name the band of colours, and explain which colour is deviated most.

figure.alt: White light entering a triangular glass prism, with the normal drawn at each face, and leaving as a spread of seven rays of different colours that reach a screen. The colours are not named.

steps.working: The white light is split into colours: the process is dispersion.
steps.decision: Refraction is the bending of one ray; dispersion is the splitting that happens because each colour is refracted by a different amount. The examiner will not accept one word for the other.

steps.working: The band of colours on the screen is a spectrum.
steps.decision: Not "rainbow": a rainbow is made in raindrops and involves a reflection as well.

steps.working: Inside the glass each colour travels at a slightly different speed.
steps.decision: That is the cause. The prism does not add colour; white light already contains all of them.

options: because different colours travel at different speeds in glass
because the prism adds colour to the light
because the screen splits the light up
whyMenu.explain: Each colour changes speed by a different amount as it enters the glass, so each is refracted by a different amount and they separate.

steps.working: violet is slowed the most, so it is refracted the most and is deviated the most.
steps.decision: Red is slowed the least, so it is deviated the least and sits at the other end of the spectrum.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The process is dispersion, the band of colours is a spectrum, and violet is deviated most because it is slowed most in the glass.

twin.stem: State which colour of the visible spectrum is refracted least by a glass prism.

accepted: red
red light
red is refracted least

items.stem: A ray of light hits a plane mirror. Which line is the angle of incidence measured from?
items.skill: Recalling the normal from the reflection topic

options.text: the normal, at right angles to the mirror
options.feedback: Yes. The same line is used for refraction, which is why reflection comes first.

options.text: the surface of the mirror
options.feedback: Angles in optics are measured from the normal, never from the surface.

options.text: the edge of the ray box
options.feedback: The angle is a property of the ray and the surface it meets, not of the equipment.

items.stem: Light travels fastest through which of these?
items.skill: Knowing that light slows in a transparent material

options.text: air
options.feedback: Yes. Light travels more slowly in glass and in water than it does in air.

options.text: glass
options.feedback: Light is slower in glass than in air, which is why it bends on the way in.

options.text: water
options.feedback: Light is slower in water than in air, though not as slow as in glass.

items.stem: White light is best described as which of these?
items.skill: Knowing that white light is a mixture

options.text: a mixture of all the colours of the visible spectrum
options.feedback: Yes, and that is why a prism can separate it.

options.text: a single colour of its own
options.feedback: White is what your eye reports when all the colours arrive together.

options.text: the absence of any colour
options.feedback: That describes darkness. White light contains every colour of the visible spectrum.

items.stem: On a graph, what does a straight line through the origin tell you about the two quantities?
items.skill: Reading proportionality from a graph, from Unit 7

options.text: they are directly proportional
options.feedback: Yes. Both conditions matter: straight, and through the origin.

options.text: they are related but not proportional
options.feedback: That is what a curve tells you. A straight line through the origin means directly proportional.

options.text: they are not related
options.feedback: A straight line is the clearest kind of relationship there is.

items.stem: A ray of light passes from air into a glass block. Which way does it bend, and why?
items.skill: Direction of bending from the change of speed

options.text: towards the normal, because it slows down
options.feedback: Yes. Slower means towards the normal; that is the whole rule.

options.text: away from the normal, because it slows down
options.feedback: Slowing down bends a ray towards the normal, not away from it.

options.text: towards the normal, because it speeds up
options.feedback: The light slows down in glass. It is the slowing that bends it towards the normal.

options.text: it does not bend, because glass is transparent
options.feedback: Transparent means the light gets through. It still changes speed at the surface, and that changes its direction.

items.stem: A diagram marks 30° between a ray and the surface of a glass block. What is the angle of incidence?
items.skill: Turning a surface angle into an angle of incidence

options.feedback: That is the angle to the surface. Subtract it from 90° to get the angle from the normal.
90° is the angle between the surface and the normal, not the angle of incidence.
Halving the printed angle is not the relationship; the printed angle and the angle of incidence add to 90°.

items.stem: Which explanation of refraction would a CCEA examiner credit?
items.skill: The change of speed, not optical density

options.text: the light changes speed as it crosses into the new material
options.feedback: Yes, and that is the exact wording the Unit 7 examiners asked for.

options.text: the glass is more optically dense than the air
options.feedback: Optical density names a property; it does not say what happens to the light. The answer wanted is the change of speed.

options.text: the light bounces off the surface of the glass
options.feedback: That is reflection. Refraction is what happens to the light that goes in.

options.text: glass is heavier than air, so it pushes the light sideways
options.feedback: Nothing pushes the light. Its speed changes, and one edge of the beam slows before the other.

items.stem: White light passes through a prism and a band of colours falls on a screen. What is that band called?

options.text: a spectrum
options.feedback: Yes. That is the word on the answer line.

options.text: a rainbow
options.feedback: A rainbow forms in raindrops and needs a reflection as well. The prism produces a spectrum.

options.text: a refraction
options.feedback: Refraction is the bending of the light, not the band of colours it produces.

options.text: a reflection
options.feedback: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. The colours here have passed through the glass.

items.stem: Which colour is refracted most by a glass prism, and why?
items.skill: Linking the amount of refraction to the change of speed

options.text: violet, because it is slowed the most in the glass
options.feedback: Yes. Most slowed means most refracted, so violet sits at the far end of the spectrum.

options.text: red, because it is slowed the most in the glass
options.feedback: Red is the colour slowed least, so it is refracted least.

options.text: violet, because it travels fastest in the glass
options.feedback: The right colour, the wrong reason: violet is refracted most because it is slowed most, not because it is fastest.

options.text: green, because it is in the middle of the spectrum
options.feedback: Being in the middle makes green neither the most nor the least refracted.

items.stem: A ray leaves a rectangular glass block through the face opposite the one it entered. How does the emergent ray compare with the incident ray?
items.skill: The two bends in a block cancel

options.text: parallel to it, but shifted sideways
options.feedback: Yes. The two bends are equal and opposite because the faces are parallel.

options.text: exactly along the same line
options.feedback: The direction comes back, but the ray has been moved sideways while it was inside the glass.

options.text: at right angles to it
options.feedback: Nothing here turns the light through a right angle; the two small bends cancel out.

options.text: spread into a spectrum
options.feedback: A rectangular block barely separates the colours, because its two faces are parallel and the bends cancel. A prism is the shape that spreads them.

items.stem: In Prescribed Practical P5, the graph of angle of refraction against angle of incidence is a curve through the origin. What should the conclusion say?
items.skill: The wording for a curve through the origin

options.text: the two angles are related but not proportional
options.feedback: Yes, and the reason to add is that the graph is a curve.

options.text: the two angles are directly proportional
options.feedback: Directly proportional needs a straight line through the origin. Through the origin alone is not enough.

options.text: the two angles are inversely proportional
options.feedback: Inversely proportional would mean one falling as the other rose; here both rise together.

options.text: nothing can be concluded from a curve
options.feedback: A curve is a real result: it says the two angles are related, just not in proportion.

hints: The word describes the splitting, not the bending.

commonErrors.feedback: Refraction is the bending of a ray of one colour. The word for white light being split into its colours is dispersion.

parts.stem:
White light from a ray box passes through a triangular glass prism and reaches a screen.
Name the process that splits the white light up.

accepted: dispersion
Dispersion

scheme.for: dispersion
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 P2 Foundation: refraction was often written where dispersion was wanted.

parts.workedSolution: Dispersion. Bending a single ray of one colour is a different idea; dispersion is the word for white light being separated into its colours because each is bent by a different amount.

hints: A rainbow is something that happens in the sky; this word is the one used for what a prism makes.

commonErrors.feedback: A rainbow is made by raindrops in the sky and involves a reflection as well. The word on the answer line is spectrum.

parts.stem: State the name given to the band of colours that appears on the screen.

accepted: spectrum
a spectrum
the visible spectrum

scheme.for: spectrum
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 P2 Foundation: "rainbow" was written instead of spectrum.

parts.workedSolution: Spectrum. The band of colours a prism throws on a screen is a spectrum; the coloured arc in the sky is made in raindrops and needs a reflection as well, so it is not the word wanted here.

hints: Count the names in the order you have learned.
parts.stem: State how many colours CCEA expects you to name in that band.
parts.workedSolution: 7: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

context.setting: The spectrum a prism throws onto a screen, from the least deviated colour to the most

hints: Start with the colour that changes speed least in the glass.
Violet is the one that has been slowed most, so it sits at the other end.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the order reversed. Red is slowed least in the glass, so it is refracted least and comes first when you start from the colour deviated the smallest amount.

parts.stem:
A prism disperses white light onto a screen.
Arrange the seven colours in the order they appear, starting with the one that has been refracted least.

scheme.for: red at the end deviated least and violet at the other end
the other five colours in the correct order between them
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2024 P2 Foundation marked the list of colours and their order as separate points.

parts.workedSolution: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Red changes speed least in the glass, so it is refracted least and is deviated the smallest amount; violet changes speed most, so it is refracted most.

hints: Start with what is different about the colours inside the glass.
Then say which colour that makes bend most.

commonErrors.feedback: Red is the colour slowed least and refracted least; violet is slowed most and refracted most. The order on the screen follows directly from that.

parts.stem: Explain why violet light is refracted more than red light by the prism. [2]

accepted: Different colours travel at different speeds in the glass, and violet is slowed the most, so it is refracted the most.
Violet changes speed more in the glass than red does, so violet is refracted the most.

scheme.for: different colours travel at different speeds in the glass
violet is slowed the most, so it is refracted the most
accept: red is slowed the least, so it is refracted the least

parts.workedSolution: Different colours travel at different speeds in the glass, and violet is slowed the most, so it is refracted the most. Red is slowed the least, so it is refracted the least.

context.setting: A ray sent into a glass block along the normal

hints: The angle of incidence is measured between the ray and the normal.

commonErrors.feedback: 90° is the angle between this ray and the surface. Measured from the normal, which is what the angle of incidence means, the answer is 0°.

parts.stem:
A ray of light is sent into a glass block along the normal, so that it meets the surface square on.
State the angle of incidence, in degrees.

scheme.for: 0 (degrees)
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2024 P2 Higher: some candidates answered 90 degrees, which is the angle to the surface.

parts.workedSolution: The ray lies along the normal, so the angle between the ray and the normal is 0°.

hints: Ask which way the ray would have to bend, and from what.

commonErrors.feedback: The light still slows down going into the glass; what does not happen is a change of direction, because the ray is already along the normal.

parts.stem: State what happens to the direction of this ray as it enters the glass, and give a reason.

accepted: It carries straight on, because it is already travelling along the normal so there is nothing to bend it away from.
The direction does not change: the ray is already along the normal, so it goes straight through.

scheme.for: the direction does not change / the ray carries straight on
because the ray is travelling along the normal (angle of incidence 0 degrees)

parts.workedSolution: It carries straight on. The ray is already travelling along the normal, so the angle of incidence is 0° and there is no bending to see, even though the light does slow down.

parts.stem:
The six steps of Prescribed Practical P5 are listed in the wrong order.
Put them in the order they should be carried out.

expectedOrder: Place the glass block on plain paper and draw round it with a sharp pencil.
Shine a single ray from the ray box at one face of the block.
Mark the ray going in and the ray coming out with two pencil crosses each.
Lift the block off the paper and join the crosses with a ruler.
Draw the normal at the point where the ray entered the block.
Measure the angles of incidence and refraction from the normal with a protractor.

white light is already a mixture of all of these colours

scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement, and the specialist words the scheme wants are dispersion, prism, spectrum and speed.

parts.workedSolution: The white light from the ray box is split by the prism into a band of colours on the screen. This splitting is called dispersion and the band is called a spectrum. Working from the colour deviated least, the order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. White light is already a mixture of all of these colours; the prism does not add anything. Each colour travels at a slightly different speed inside the glass, so each is refracted by a slightly different amount and they separate. Red is slowed the least, so it is refracted the least. Violet is slowed the most, so it is refracted the most.

hints: The independent variable is the one you decide to change.
parts.stem:
In Prescribed Practical P5 the student changes one quantity and measures another.
Identify the independent variable.

options.text: the angle of incidence
options.feedback: Correct: that is the one the student chooses and changes.

options.text: the angle of refraction
options.feedback: That is the one measured as a result, so it is the dependent variable.

options.text: the glass block
options.feedback: The block is kept the same throughout, so it is a control variable.

options.text: the brightness of the ray box
options.feedback: The brightness is kept the same and is not measured, so it is a control variable.

scheme.for: the angle of incidence

parts.workedSolution: The angle of incidence: the student sets it, and the angle of refraction is what they measure in response.

hints: Look at how far apart the three angles are.
Say what a wider spread would let the student do with the graph.

commonErrors.feedback: Repeating each reading improves reliability, which is worth having, but the problem here is the range: three angles close together cannot show the shape of the curve.

parts.stem:
The student's angles of incidence were 20°, 30° and 40°.
Suggest one improvement to this set of readings, and give a reason. [2]

accepted: Take readings over a wider range of angles, because three readings bunched together cannot show the shape of the graph.
Use more angles of incidence up to about 70 degrees, so that the curve can be seen over the whole range.

scheme.for: take readings over a wider range of angles of incidence / add more angles
so that the shape of the graph can be seen across the whole range
accept: so the curve can be drawn properly
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 Unit 7 Booklet B: a value was left out of the range of readings and the mark was forfeited.

parts.workedSolution: Take readings over a wider range of angles of incidence, up to about 70°, because three readings bunched together cannot show the shape of the graph.

hints: Less bending means a smaller change of speed.
Say which material the light travels faster in.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the angle the ray would refract to in glass. Water slows light less than glass does, so the ray bends less and the angle of refraction is larger.

parts.stem:
The student repeats the experiment with a water cell instead of the glass block. At an angle of incidence of 55° the angle of refraction in the water is 38°, which is larger than the 35° measured in glass at 60°.
State the angle of refraction in the water, in degrees, and say what the comparison tells you about the speed of light in water compared with glass.

scheme.for: 38 (degrees)
water refracts the light less than glass does
so light is slowed less in water: it travels faster in water than in glass
scheme.examinerNote: The specification's rule, in short: the more the light is refracted, the bigger its change of speed.

parts.workedSolution: The angle of refraction in the water is 38°. Water refracts the light less than glass does, so the light is slowed less in water, which means light travels faster in water than in glass.

parts.stem:
The graph shows a student's P5 results for a water cell.
Describe how the two angles are linked, as the graph shows them.

options.text: they are related but not proportional
options.feedback: Correct, and that is the wording the scheme wants.

options.text: they are directly proportional
options.feedback: Directly proportional means a straight line through the origin. This graph passes through the origin but curves, so the angles are related but not proportional.

options.text: they are independent of each other
options.feedback: As the angle of incidence increases so does the angle of refraction, so they are related. What they are not is proportional.

options.text: they are inversely proportional
options.feedback: Inversely proportional would mean one falls as the other rises. Here both rise together.

scheme.for: related but not proportional

parts.workedSolution: They are related but not proportional: both angles increase together, but the graph is a curve rather than a straight line through the origin.

commonErrors.feedback: The plotted line is a curve. A straight line through the origin is what would have shown the two angles were directly proportional, and this graph does not have that shape.

parts.stem: Give a reason, from the shape of the graph, for your answer to part (a).

accepted: The graph is a curve, not a straight line through the origin.
Because the line is curved rather than straight.
It is not a straight line through the origin; it curves.

scheme.for: the graph is a curve / it is not a straight line through the origin
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 Unit 7 Booklet A Higher: most chose related but not proportional, but few could give a reason; a statement that the graph is a curve, or not a straight line through the origin, was all that was needed. The scheme made this mark depend on the right box.

parts.workedSolution: The graph is a curve, not a straight line through the origin, so the two angles are related but not proportional.

scheme.for: 32 (degrees); accept 31 to 33

parts.workedSolution: Go across from 45° on the vertical axis to the curve, then down to the horizontal axis: about 32°.

parts.stem:
The ray meets the top face of the block at an angle of incidence of 60°. Inside the glass it travels at 35° to the normal.
State the angle of refraction, in degrees.

scheme.for: 35 (degrees)
scheme.examinerNote: The angle of refraction is the one inside the new material, measured from the normal there.

parts.workedSolution: The angle of refraction is the angle inside the glass, measured from the normal: 35°.

commonErrors.feedback: Optical density is a name for a property, not an explanation. Say that the light slows down, and then which way that bends it.

parts.stem: Explain, in terms of the speed of the light, why the ray bends as it enters the block.

accepted: The light slows down as it goes into the glass, so it is refracted towards the normal.
Its speed decreases in the glass, and that change of speed bends the ray towards the normal.

scheme.for: the light slows down / its speed decreases on entering the glass
so it bends towards the normal

parts.workedSolution: The light slows down as it goes into the glass, so it is refracted towards the normal. The bigger the change of speed, the bigger the bend.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the angle inside the glass. On the way out the light speeds up and bends away from the normal, back to 60°.

parts.stem:
The ray reaches the bottom face and leaves the block.
State the angle between the emergent ray and the normal at the bottom face, in degrees.

scheme.for: 60 (degrees)

parts.workedSolution: The faces are parallel, so the ray leaves at the angle it entered at: 60°.

commonErrors.feedback: Leaving the glass the light speeds up, and speeding up bends a ray away from the normal.

parts.stem: Describe how the ray changes direction as it leaves the block, and how the emergent ray compares with the ray that entered.

accepted: It speeds up and bends away from the normal, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.
The light bends away from the normal as it leaves, and the emergent ray is parallel to the ray that went in, shifted sideways.

scheme.for: it speeds up and bends away from the normal
the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray

parts.workedSolution: At the bottom face the light speeds up and bends away from the normal, by exactly as much as it bent towards it on the way in. So the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, shifted sideways.

emphasis: greater refraction, greater change of speed

parts.stem:
In Prescribed Practical P5 the student changes one quantity and measures another.
Identify the independent variable.

options.text: the angle of incidence
options.feedback: Correct: that is the one the student chooses and changes.

options.text: the angle of refraction
options.feedback: That is the one measured as a result, so it is the dependent variable.

options.text: the glass block
options.feedback: The block is kept the same throughout, so it is a control variable.

options.text: the brightness of the ray box
options.feedback: The brightness is kept the same and is not measured, so it is a control variable.

scheme.for: the angle of incidence

parts.workedSolution: The angle of incidence: the student sets it, and the angle of refraction is what they measure in response.

commonErrors.feedback: Repeating each reading improves reliability, which is worth having, but the problem here is the range: three angles close together cannot show the shape of the graph.

parts.stem:
The student's angles of incidence were 20°, 30° and 40°.
Suggest one improvement to this set of readings, and give a reason.

accepted: Take readings over a wider range of angles, up to about 70 degrees, so that the shape of the graph can be seen.
Use more angles of incidence from 0 up to 70 degrees, so the curve can be seen over the whole range.

scheme.for: take readings over a wider range of angles of incidence / add more angles
so that the shape of the graph can be seen across the whole range
accept: so the curve can be drawn properly
scheme.examinerNote: Three readings bunched between 20° and 40° cannot show whether the graph curves; the P5 tables CCEA prints run from 0° up to 70° or 80° (Summer 2021 and Summer 2025 Unit 7 Booklet A).

parts.workedSolution: Take readings over a wider range of angles of incidence, from 0° up to about 70°, because three readings bunched together cannot show the shape of the graph.

commonErrors.feedback: The larger angle of refraction, 38° in water, means less bending, not more. The glass bends the ray closer to the normal, so the glass refracts more.

State which material refracts the light more.

prompts.prompt: What is the normal, and what is it used for in a refraction diagram?
prompts.answer: A line at right angles to the surface, drawn where the ray meets it. Both angles are measured from the normal: the angle of incidence on one side and the angle of refraction on the other.

prompts.prompt: Light goes from air into glass. Which way does it bend, and what causes the bend?
prompts.answer: It bends towards the normal, because it slows down as it enters the glass. A change of speed is what changes the direction.

prompts.prompt: A diagram marks an angle between a ray and the surface of a block. What must you do before you use it?
prompts.answer: Subtract it from 90 degrees. The surface and the normal are at right angles, and every angle in optics is measured from the normal.

prompts.prompt: What is dispersion, and what is the band of colours it produces called?
prompts.answer: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its colours by a prism, because each colour travels at a different speed in the glass. The band of colours is called a spectrum.

prompts.prompt: In the spectrum from a prism, which colour is refracted least and which most, and why?
prompts.answer: Red is refracted least because it is slowed the least in the glass, and violet is refracted most because it is slowed the most.

prompts.prompt: List the seven colours of the spectrum in order, starting with the one refracted least.
prompts.answer: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet

prompts.prompt: Describe the method of Prescribed Practical P5 in one sentence.
prompts.answer: Draw round a glass block on paper, shine a single ray in and mark the ray going in and coming out, lift the block, join the marks, draw the normal, and measure both angles with a protractor.

prompts.prompt: What does the P5 graph of angle of refraction against angle of incidence show, and why?
prompts.answer: That the two angles are related but not proportional, because the graph is a curve rather than a straight line through the origin.

prompts.prompt: A ray goes in one face of a rectangular glass block and out the opposite face. How does the emergent ray compare with the incident ray?
prompts.answer: It is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways, because the two faces are parallel so the two bends are equal and opposite.

prompts.prompt: A straw in a glass of water looks broken at the surface. Explain why, using the word speed.
prompts.answer: Light from the part of the straw under the water slows down in the water and changes direction as it leaves, so it reaches your eye from a direction the straw is not really in.
